title: Kinematics
final_note: You worked through the key terms in Kinematics.

concepts.def: Displacement s (vector); velocity v = ds/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt = d²s/dt². All are vectors in 2D/3D.
For constant acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ((u+v)/2)t. Useful when a is constant.
Speed is scalar (magnitude of velocity). Velocity is vector — has direction.
If a depends on t: v = ∫a dt; s = ∫v dt. Use calculus rather than SUVAT.
Slope = acceleration; area under graph = displacement. Helpful for visualising motion.
Take a = g = 9.8 m/s² downward (or 9.81). Use SUVAT for projectiles, free fall.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Kinematics — a core area of A-Level Maths.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Kinematics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Kinematics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A particle starts from rest and accelerates at 4 m/s² for 3 seconds. Final velocity is:
options: 12 m/s
7 m/s

mcqs.q: Which SUVAT equation does NOT involve t?
options: v² = u² + 2as
v = u + at
s = ut + ½at²

mcqs.q: If 6 workers take 8 hours to paint a wall, how long would 12 workers take (assuming they work at the same rate)?
options: Yes, because the 2 represents how many times x appears.
8 hours, because each worker still has to do the same job.
16 hours, because doubling the workers doubles everything including the time.
4 hours — this is inverse proportion: double the workers, halve the time.

mcqs.q: Is 2x the same as x squared (x^2)?
options: Yes, because both involve the number 2 and the letter x.
Yes, because the 2 represents how many times x appears.
No — 2x means x + x (or 2 times x); x^2 means x times x.
y equals 1 because the numerator stays the same.

mcqs.q: What does the graph of y = 1/x do as x approaches 0?
options: y goes to plus or minus infinity — the graph has a vertical asymptote at x = 0.
y equals 1 because the numerator stays the same.
Yes, because the 2 represents how many times x appears.
y equals 0 because dividing 1 by something small is small.
